extracted.intended_audience: K-12 teachers, curriculum designers, and media literacy educators/policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: A framework of core new-media literacy competencies educators should teach (collective intelligence, judgment, transmedia navigation, networking) with examples and classroom activities to develop those skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective intelligence / collaborative problem-solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to work as part of large-scale knowledge communities that pool observations, share expertise across domains and geographies, and collaboratively solve problems (the text: 'The solutions do not lie in the puzzles... they lie in the connections we make').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include alternate reality games (I Love Bees, Cloudmakers) where thousands collaborate (answering pay-phone calls, feeding clues into online tools). Guidance notes the need to train newcomers, use online collaboration tools, and that such communities can tackle problems beyond any individual’s capacity (e.g., mapping Hurricane Katrina damage). Also notes the potential for error and the communal processes for refining or dismissing misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership within knowledge communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders must identify specific functions for each team member based on expertise and interact with members appropriately ('Leadership within a knowledge community requires the ability to identify specific functions for each member of the team based on his or her expertise').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classroom implication: assign roles (biologist, detective, technologist) so participants use different tools and have incentives to pool resources (example: MIT museum whodunit with parent-child pairs). Emphasizes appropriate interaction styles and role assignment as a leadership skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinarity and role specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Teamwork involves a high degree of interdisciplinarity—reconfiguring knowledge across traditional categories of expertise and assigning distinct roles that give access to different information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Games and cooperative learning that assign distinct roles (each with different tools) create incentives to share findings. Schools should allow students to assume roles based on emerging expertise rather than only striving for generalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance individual responsibility and group ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must learn to function both as autonomous problem solvers and as members of collaborative communities; schools often teach individual ownership ('turn in their own work') but collective intelligence encourages group ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical tension: schools grade individuals while knowledge communities encourage shared ownership. Instruction should teach students to thrive in both worlds—maintain broad background knowledge while knowing when to tap community expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment: evaluate reliability and credibility of information sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to evaluate the reliability and credibility of different information sources, including understanding that knowledge produced in collective settings is 'always in process' and may contain errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should learn to cross-check, vet, and place a piece of information within its vetting process to decide how much trust to place in it. Tools and practices: comparing Wikipedia and Encyclopedia Britannica (Nature study), using Snopes, Ligit, and Talk pages, and participating in wiki construction to learn about production processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand vetting processes and provenance of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Know how and where information is produced, how it is vetted or corrected, and how that affects trust ('understanding the current placement within the vetting process helps determine how much trust to place in any given piece of information').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wikis work best with many active participants; some articles attract thousands of editors while others may remain erroneous for months. Instruction should cultivate intuitive sense of production contexts and mechanisms of correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance trust in traditional gatekeepers with grassroots self-correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when to trust established institutions (editors, journalists, public broadcasters) and when grassroots, citizen-journalist or community-led correction may be more accurate ('We need to balance a trust of traditional gatekeeping organizations ... with the self-correcting potential of grassroots knowledge communities').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage reading multiple sources against each other; teach that established media can err and that bloggers/community efforts sometimes detect flaws in mainstream reporting (example: bloggers identifying flaws in 60 Minutes coverage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fact from fiction and argument from documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to distinguish fact from fiction, argument from documentation, real from fake, and marketing from enlightenment ('The new mediated landscape ... demands that students be taught how to distinguish fact from ﬁction, argument from documentation, real from fake, and marketing from enlightenment').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to ask basic critical questions about what they watch, read, or hear. Classroom activities: ranking news stories by traditional news standards, underlining framing words in articles, and exercises that make arguments explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify producer perspective and motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze who is presenting what to whom and why; identify perspectives, interests, and mechanisms that shape representations ('it is vital for students to also identify and analyze the perspective of the producer').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use media-literacy materials that examine intentions and effects behind controversial media properties; teach students to detect the motives behind websites and distinguish commercial from noncommercial content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participatory practice to learn credibility (learn-by-doing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students learn judgment by participating in the production and correction of content (e.g., contributing to wikis, reflecting on inaccuracies), not just by passive consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities: contribute to Wikipedia and analyze Talk Pages, practice editing and correcting entries, and reflect on how inaccuracies are introduced and resolved; use Ligit and Snopes to practice flagging suspect content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmedia navigation: follow stories across multiple modalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to follow the flow of stories and information across multiple media (identify same content translated across modes, understand narrative logic across media, and synthesize dispersed elements into a coherent understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pokémon as a phenomenon 'you do'—information assembled from TV, games, cards; exercises: trace a fairy tale across media and historical contexts; MIT exercise to tell the same story across IM, PowerPoint, video, drawings to see what must remain constant for recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design literacy / multimodality: express ideas across modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Be equally adept at reading and writing across images, text, sound, and simulations; choose modes and techniques that best convey meaning to specific audiences ('students must learn to sort through a range of different possible modes of expression').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach composition beyond written text to include design literacy. Classroom examples: image-manipulation activities to see how meaning changes, using The Sims 2 for role-play storytelling, and designing outputs across media (film, graphics, audio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Networking: search for, synthesize, and disseminate information
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to navigate social and algorithmic search systems, tap collective intelligence, and disseminate findings; being resourceful in locating and sharing relevant information across networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists and explains platforms (Google, Amazon, Movielens, eBay, Del.icio.us, Answers.google, Citeulike, Last.fm, RSS) and their different affordances (link analysis, recommendation by similar users, reputation systems, bookmarking patterns). Emphasizes understanding how knowledge is generated on each platform and analyzing social/psychological factors shaping collective behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose search systems and network strategies matched to information goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which group or search system is most likely to surface relevant resources and select systems based on criteria (similar tastes, divergent viewpoints, popularity, trusted third-party assessment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classroom practice: Webquests that require students to use curated web resources and synthesize perspectives; teach students to choose search strategies aligned to specific needs (e.g., expert communities vs general popularity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesize multiple sources and apply 'wisdom of crowds' principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine multiple resources to produce new knowledge and understand the conditions that make crowds smart: diversity, decentralization, a way to aggregate opinions, and independence ('There are four key qualities that make a crowd smart').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should cultivate diverse and decentralized contributions, teach aggregation methods, and preserve independence of contributors. Classroom implication: design collaborative tasks that maximize these conditions to improve collective outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pedagogical activities to build competencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ concrete classroom activities (image-manipulation, Webquests, mapping local government, eelgrass data projects, transmedia storytelling, museum whodunits) to teach the above skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: mapping Hurricane Katrina with user-submitted overlays; students cultivating eelgrass and sharing nitrate/oxygen data; Mandarin students creating travel guides via Ning; New Media Literacies exercises (storytelling across media), Youth Voice Collaborative news-ranking activity; use of Google News to compare framings.
